common_name: Kanzi Apple (Gala x Braeburn Crisp Sweet-Tart Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring while dormant, in well-drained fertile soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator such as Gala or Golden Delicious nearby for reliable fruit set.

directions: Kanzi was bred in Belgium from a cross of Gala and Braeburn, combining Gala's crisp sweetness with a firmer texture and a brighter, more tart edge from its Braeburn parent. Fruit ripens in mid-to-late season, well after Gala, and colors to a deep red blush over a yellow-green background. It stores considerably longer than Gala thanks to its dense flesh, and the tree crops reliably once established. Thin clusters to one fruit each in early summer for larger, better-colored apples.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; the naturally columnar growth habit needs little pruning and suits small yards, patios, and large containers.

directions: Rockit was developed in New Zealand as a naturally dwarf, columnar apple that produces clusters of small, snack-sized fruit along a single upright trunk rather than wide spreading branches. The fruit is sweet, crisp, and red-striped, sized to be eaten in a couple of bites, and the compact habit makes it one of the few apple cultivars practical for container growing on a patio. Because it stays narrow, plant it closer than a standard apple and provide a compatible pollinator within range for good fruit set. Thin overcrowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit size.

common_name: Modi Apple (Gala x Liberty Disease-Resistant Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; its inherited scab resistance makes it a good option for low-spray home orchards in humid climates.

directions: Modi was bred in Italy from a cross of Gala and Liberty, pairing Gala's sweet, crisp eating quality with Liberty's strong resistance to apple scab. The deep red, almost fully colored fruit ripens in the fall a few weeks after Gala and holds its crunch well in storage. Its disease-resistant parentage lets home growers get a clean, attractive crop with far less fungicide spraying than scab-susceptible varieties require. Provide a compatible pollinator nearby, since it is not self-fertile.

common_name: Smitten Apple (New Zealand Bred Sweet Crisp Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator within range for good fruit set.

directions: Smitten was bred by Plant and Food Research in New Zealand and selected for its dense, juicy crunch, honeyed sweetness, and appealing bright yellow skin with a pink-red blush. It ripens in the early-to-mid fall harvest window and keeps its crisp texture well in cold storage. The tree tends to bear at a relatively young age once established. Thin fruit clusters in early summer to improve fruit size and reduce the tendency toward biennial bearing.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; its resistance to apple scab makes it a strong choice for organic and low-spray orchards.

directions: Pinata, also sold as Sonata in some markets, was bred in Germany from parentage that includes Cox's Orange Pippin, Duchess of Oldenburg, and Golden Delicious, and it was selected specifically for durable resistance to apple scab. The yellow-orange, red-striped fruit ripens in early-to-mid fall with a sweet, aromatic flavor reminiscent of its Cox ancestry, though milder and less complex. It stores reasonably well for a mid-season apple and crops reliably once established. Provide a compatible pollinator, since it is not self-fertile.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator within range for good fruit set.

directions: Junami was bred by the Swiss agricultural research institute Agroscope and selected for its crisp, juicy bite and aromatic, floral sweetness. The fruit has a distinctive bright red-orange blush over a pale yellow background and ripens in the mid-to-late fall. It handles cold storage well without losing its crunch and the tree crops at a moderate, manageable rate. Thin fruit clusters in early summer for the best size and to encourage annual rather than biennial bearing.

common_name: Karmijn de Sonnaville Apple (Dutch Rich-Flavored Heirloom Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in a warm, sheltered, well-drained site in full sun; this cultivar can be susceptible to scab and benefits from good air circulation and a preventive spray program in humid regions.

directions: Karmijn de Sonnaville was raised in the Netherlands in 1949 by Piet de Sonnaville from a cross of Jonathan and Belle de Boskoop, producing a russeted, red-striped apple prized among connoisseurs for its intensely rich, wine-like, sweet-tart flavor. The tree is somewhat vigorous and can bear biennially without careful thinning, and its Boskoop parentage leaves it more prone to scab than many modern cultivars. Because of its demanding growth habits it rewards attentive home orchardists more than commercial growers seeking easy, uniform crops. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once the fruit develops its characteristic red blush over a green-gold background.

common_name: Fiesta Apple (Red Pippin, English Cox's Orange Pippin Successor)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Fiesta crops more reliably and needs less disease management than its Cox's Orange Pippin parent.

directions: Fiesta, also marketed as Red Pippin, was bred at England's East Malling Research Station from a cross of Cox's Orange Pippin and Idared, aiming to capture some of Cox's celebrated complex flavor in a hardier, more dependable tree. The red-flushed fruit ripens in mid-to-late fall with crisp, juicy flesh and a balanced sweet-sharp flavor milder than Golden Delicious but brighter than most dessert apples. It bears more consistently and resists disease better than Cox's Orange Pippin, making it a practical choice for home gardeners who want Cox-like flavor without Cox's finicky reputation. Provide a compatible pollinator, since it is not self-fertile.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Suncrisp ripens late and benefits from a long, warm growing season to fully develop its sugars.

directions: Suncrisp was developed by the Rutgers University apple breeding program in New Jersey and released for its yellow, sometimes red-blushed fruit with a sweet-tart, Golden Delicious-like flavor and notably crisp, juicy flesh. It ripens late in the season, generally after Golden Delicious, and stores exceptionally well in cold storage, holding its texture and flavor for months. The tree tends to bear heavily and may need fruit thinning in early summer to keep fruit size up and prevent limb breakage. Provide a compatible pollinator, since it is not self-fertile.

common_name: Autumn Glory Apple (Caramel-Flavored Very Late Keeper Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Autumn Glory ripens very late and needs a long, warm autumn to fully develop its characteristic flavor and color.

directions: Autumn Glory was discovered and developed by Broetje Orchards in Washington State and is notable for a distinctive caramel and cinnamon-spice flavor unlike most dessert apples, layered over a sweet, dense, crisp bite. It is one of the last apples to ripen each season, typically harvested in late October, and its firm flesh keeps in cold storage for many months without losing quality. The tree bears reliably once established and colors to a deep red over most of the fruit surface. Provide a compatible pollinator nearby, since it is not self-fertile.

common_name: SnowSweet Apple (University of Minnesota Non-Browning White-Flesh Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; SnowSweet is bred for cold hardiness and suits the harsh winters of the northern growing region the University of Minnesota program targets.

directions: SnowSweet was released by the University of Minnesota apple breeding program and is distinguished by its unusually slow-browning white flesh, which stays fresh-looking far longer than most apples once cut, making it popular for lunchboxes and fruit trays. The mildly sweet, low-acid flavor and dense, crisp texture pair with a red-blushed skin over a pale background, and fruit ripens in the fall. The tree is bred for the extreme winter cold of the Upper Midwest and is reliably hardy well into colder zones than most dessert apples. Thin fruit clusters in early summer for larger apples and more consistent annual bearing.

common_name: Falstaff Apple (English James Grieve x Golden Delicious Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Falstaff is partially self-fertile but produces heavier crops with a compatible pollinator nearby.

directions: Falstaff was bred at England's East Malling Research Station from a cross of James Grieve and Golden Delicious, producing a compact, reliably cropping tree well suited to smaller home gardens. The fruit ripens in early-to-mid fall with crisp, juicy flesh and a balanced sweet-sharp flavor milder than Golden Delicious but brighter than most dessert apples. It is a dependable, easy-care variety that tolerates a range of soils and needs relatively little disease management compared with older English heirlooms. Harvest when the greenish-yellow skin develops a light orange-red flush and fruit separates easily from the spur.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Greensleeves is self-fertile and reliably productive even as a single tree in a small garden.

directions: Greensleeves was bred at East Malling Research Station in England from the same James Grieve and Golden Delicious cross that produced Falstaff, and it was selected for its dependable, heavy cropping and self-fertility, meaning a single tree can set fruit without a separate pollinator nearby. The pale green-yellow fruit ripens in early-to-mid fall with crisp, juicy, mildly sweet-tart flesh good for both fresh eating and cooking. Because it bears young and abundantly, thin fruit clusters in early summer to prevent overcropping and biennial bearing. It has become one of the most widely recommended apples for small English gardens for exactly these easy-care traits.

common_name: Chivers Delight Apple (English Late-Season Cox-Type Dessert Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chivers Delight ripens late and stores well, so allow full hang time before harvest for the best flavor.

directions: Chivers Delight was raised in Cambridgeshire, England, by fruit grower Stewart Chivers and selected for its rich, aromatic, Cox-like flavor in a more reliably productive tree than Cox's Orange Pippin itself. The yellow-green, red-striped fruit ripens late in the season and develops a dense, sweet, complex flavor that improves after several weeks in storage. It is a good option for gardeners who love Cox's flavor profile but want a hardier, more consistent cropper. Provide a compatible pollinator nearby, since it is not self-fertile.

common_name: Red Windsor Apple (English Red-Skinned Cox-Flavored Dessert Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator within range for good fruit set.

directions: Red Windsor is a modern English dessert apple selected for combining a richly aromatic, Cox-like flavor with a much more reliable, heavier-cropping habit and a fully red-flushed skin that colors easily even in cooler summers. Fruit ripens in mid-to-late fall with firm, juicy, sweet-tart flesh that holds its quality well in storage. It tends to bear consistent annual crops rather than the biennial pattern common in older Cox-type apples. Harvest once the skin has fully colored and the fruit separates easily from the spur.

common_name: Herefordshire Russet Apple (Disease-Resistant Nutty Russet Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; its scab and mildew resistance makes it well suited to organic and low-spray home orchards.

directions: Herefordshire Russet was bred by the English nursery Frank P. Matthews from a cross involving Egremont Russet, aiming to combine classic russet flavor with stronger resistance to apple scab and powdery mildew than older russet varieties typically offer. The golden-brown, rough-skinned fruit ripens in mid fall with a dry, nutty, honeyed flavor characteristic of russet apples. Because it needs less fungicide intervention than many heirloom russets, it is a practical choice for home growers in humid regions where scab pressure is high. Provide a compatible pollinator, since it is not self-fertile.

common_name: Saturn Apple (English Scab-Resistant Golden Delicious-Type Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Saturn's strong scab resistance makes it a reliable low-spray choice for humid climates.

directions: Saturn was bred in England as part of a disease-resistance breeding program and carries strong resistance to apple scab, one of the most damaging fungal diseases of apples in humid climates. The medium-sized, red-flushed fruit over a pale yellow-green background ripens in early-to-mid fall with a crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor reminiscent of Golden Delicious. Its clean disease record makes it a dependable choice for organic and low-input home orchards. Provide a compatible pollinator nearby, since it is not self-fertile.
